source.title_on_document: Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs: Randomized Experiments on Divergent and Convergent Thinking

supplement.where: Appendix A (Experiment 1) and Appendix B (Experiment 2) at the end of this PDF, pp. 16-18; the main text points to their Figures 11 and 12. No separate online supplement is mentioned. The two preregistrations are separate documents: https://aspredicted.org/dkvp-n785.pdf (Experiment 1, p. 4 footnote 1) and https://aspredicted.org/4q75-bskd.pdf (Experiment 2, p. 9 footnote 2).
supplement.holds: GPT-4o settings (gpt-4o, August 2024, temperature 0, top-p 0.95, max response 4000 in Experiment 1 and 800 in Experiment 2), input prompts, system prompts (Figures 11 and 12), and sample LLM responses (Tables 1 and 2). No statistics. All test statistics are in the main text, and the paper has no results tables: arm sizes, arm means, SDs, and standard errors are not printed. Arm levels appear only as plotted points in Figures 4, 5, and 9; only the Figure 5 caption says what its error bars show (one standard error of the mean).

paper_design_summary: Two preregistered, between-subjects online experiments on Prolific (460 and 640 participants recruited, US or UK) randomly assigned each person to no AI, a standard GPT-4o output (a list of seven ideas, or the answer), or a coach-like GPT-4o output (seven SCAMPER-style prompts, or associated words) for three exposure rounds. After a one-minute Snake game, everyone did one (Experiment 1) or two (Experiment 2) more rounds of the same task without AI. Experiment 1 used the Alternate Uses Test and scored ideas for originality (fine-tuned GPT-3 classifier), number of ideas, and SBERT distances within a person's ideas, between test-round and exposure-round ideas, and across people; Experiment 2 used the Remote Associates Test and scored accuracy.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Type of GPT-4o response shown during the three exposure rounds of the AUT: None, List of Ideas (seven sampled GPT-4o alternate uses), or List of Strategies (seven SCAMPER-based prompts with no answers). The test round was unassisted for everyone.
assignment.quote: During the exposure phase, participants are introduced to three objects, one after the other. Every participant was randomly assigned to receive one of three types of LLM responses:
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1.1; p. 4, Section 3.1 ('three-condition, between-subjects experiment'); p. 4, Figure 2 ('Randomize Condition', '33.3% each')
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 4, footnote 1 (https://aspredicted.org/dkvp-n785.pdf; AsPredicted #189,206, registered 2024/09/07); p. 6, Section 3.1.4 ('Following our pre-registration')

arms.name: None
arms.description: Control group. No LLM support provided. Also labeled 'No LLM Response' (Figure 2; Section 3.2).

arms.name: List of Ideas
arms.description: GPT-4o generated alternate uses for the object; seven randomly sampled uses (from a pool of 20 per object, p. 8) were shown, which participants could freely use in their responses. Figure 3 labels this panel 'LLM Answer'.

arms.name: List of Strategies
arms.description: GPT-4o with a SCAMPER system prompt (Figure 11) generated seven strategies; it guided participants without sharing explicit answers. Figure 3 labels this panel 'LLM Guidance'.

participants.exclusions: Not stated in the paper. Figure 2 shows n = 460 entering consent and randomization (33.3% each) with no attrition shown; the paper prints no per-arm counts, no exclusions, and no count of people analyzed, and it mentions no attention check for this experiment. Results cover '9,457 ideas generated by participants across all conditions and phases' (p. 6); the Limitations round this to '10,000 ideas' (p. 14). The preregistration (item 6) planned to exclude attention-check failures and non-completers.
participants.who: Prolific participants based in the US or UK and fluent in English; paid $1.57 for about 12 minutes
participants.locator: p. 6, Section 3.1.5; p. 4, Figure 2 (n = 460); p. 6, Section 3.2 (9,457 ideas)

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o (gpt-4o, date of use August 2024; temperature 0; top-p 0.95; max response 4000; frequency and presence penalty 0)
ai_tool.how_used: Static response panel, not an interactive chat. Five seconds after each object appeared, the assigned GPT-4o response streamed character by character beside the idea entry box. List of Ideas: seven sampled GPT-4o uses that participants could freely use (ideas_supplied). List of Strategies: seven SCAMPER prompts with no examples (coach). The role field records the standard arm. No LLM support in the test round. Settings in Appendix A.1, p. 16.

task.description: Alternate Uses Test: list creative uses for everyday objects (sampled from tire, pants, shoe, table, bottle), submitting ideas one by one. Three exposure rounds with the assigned GPT-4o response, a one-minute Snake distractor game, then one test round on a new object with no AI for anyone.
task.duration: Two minutes per object; about 12 minutes for the whole experiment

outcomes.name: Originality, test round (unassisted)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality of each AUT idea scored 1-5 by an existing fine-tuned GPT-3 classifier (Organisciak et al. 2023 [44]) trained on human 1-5 originality judgments; r = 0.81 with human judgments overall, r > 0.88 for the five objects used. Kruskal-Wallis H test across the three arms, then Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction. The paper does not say whether the tests run on idea scores or participant means; Figure 4a plots the average originality of ideas. Preregistered main question and key dependent variable (AsPredicted #189,206, items 2-3).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after a one-minute Snake distractor game

contrasts.reported: Omnibus Kruskal-Wallis (three arms) H(2) = 9.14, p = 0.010; Dunn (Bonferroni) List of Strategies vs no LLM exposure p = 0.009 ('performed significantly worse'). Arm levels only in Figure 4a.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 3.2.1 (Test phase paragraph); p. 7, Figure 4a

outcomes.name: Fluency (number of ideas), exposure rounds (AI available)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas the participant generated per exposure round. Each person has three exposure rounds, and the paper does not say whether the test uses one value per participant-round (three per person) or one mean per person. The unit is coded participant, the nearest code under either reading, because the codebook has no participant-round code. Kruskal-Wallis H test with Dunn's post-hoc test (Bonferroni). List of Ideas participants 'submitted nearly two fewer ideas than what was shown to them on average per round' (seven shown).

outcomes.name: Group-level diversity of ideas, test round (unassisted)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Simulated group diversity: ideas sampled across participants by condition, item, and phase; 150 Monte Carlo runs, each sampling 7 ideas per round and taking the median pairwise cosine distance of their SBERT embeddings (higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal). The paper does not say whether the 150 runs are per condition and phase, per round, or per item, so the number of set-level values per arm is not stated. Section 3.1.4 says the Kruskal-Wallis and Dunn procedure was applied to group-level diversity, but no statistic is printed for the test phase. Preregistered as an additional analysis (AsPredicted #189,206, item 8).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after a one-minute Snake distractor game

contrasts.reported: No statistic printed. Text: participants exposed to LLM-generated strategies 'continued to generate more similar ideas in the test phase, even without LLM assistance, a phenomenon known as homogenization'. Figure 5b: List of Strategies lowest in the test phase; error bars one SE of the mean.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Section 3.2.4 (group-level paragraphs); p. 7, Figure 5b; p. 13, Section 5.1.3

contrasts.reported: No statistic printed. Figure 5b plots List of Ideas below None in the test phase (the one-SE bars do not overlap), and the Discussion says 'participants with no LLM interactions in the study collectively generated the most diverse idea sets (Figure 5)'. It also says 'The List of Ideas condition did not lead to the same lasting homogenization once the LLM was no longer present', a comparison with List of Strategies.

diversity_detail.metric: Median pairwise cosine distance between SBERT embeddings of 7 ideas sampled across participants, averaged over 150 Monte Carlo runs
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SBERT (Reimers and Gurevych 2019 [49]); checkpoint not stated
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs within each random sample of 7 ideas drawn across participants of one condition, for a given item and phase, over 150 Monte Carlo runs. The paper says 'This sampling process reflects the number of participants in each condition' and does not explain it.
diversity_detail.uncertainty: No test printed for the test phase. Error bars are one standard error of the mean (Figure 5 caption); the paper does not say over what they are computed, and the values come from Monte Carlo runs, not participants.
diversity_detail.notes: Sign: higher = more diverse. The paper calls the List of Strategies result persistent homogenization (p. 8; p. 13).

outcomes.measure_detail: Same Monte Carlo SBERT measure as S1-O7, on exposure-round ideas (150 Monte Carlo runs; number of set-level values per arm not stated). Figure 5b.

Similar across all conditions (p > 0.05)

diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs within each random sample of 7 ideas drawn across participants of one condition, for a given item and phase, over 150 Monte Carlo runs

outcomes.name: Creative flexibility (dissimilarity of test-round ideas to exposure-round ideas)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: The paper's 'creative flexibility' (also called p-creativity): for each test-round idea, the maximum cosine similarity between its embedding and all the ideas in the Exposure set, reported so that a higher value means more dissimilarity (Figure 4c). The paper implies, but does not state, that the Exposure set holds the participant's own exposure-round ideas (Figure 4 caption: 'participant creative flexibility'). Coded flexibility, the paper's own name, under codebook Section 6 ('Variety among one person's own ideas is flexibility'), as for S1-O5 and S1-O6. Novelty is the alternative reading, because p-creativity means ideas novel to the individual (p. 3). The score is defined per idea, and the paper does not say whether the test runs on idea scores or participant means, so the unit is coded output, as for S1-O1. Kruskal-Wallis H test with Dunn's post-hoc test (Bonferroni). Not in the preregistration.
outcomes.delay: Same session, after a one-minute Snake distractor game

contrasts.reported: Omnibus Kruskal-Wallis H(2) = 6.31, p = 0.043; Dunn (Bonferroni) pairwise comparisons 'did not reach significance after correcting for multiple comparisons'; List of Strategies directionally more similar to the exposure-round ideas (lower flexibility), p = 0.052 vs No LLM Response
contrasts.locator: pp. 7-8, Section 3.2.3 (statistics on p. 8); p. 7, Figure 4c

contrasts.reported: Omnibus H(2) = 6.31, p = 0.043; pairwise comparisons did not reach significance; no p printed for this pair. Figure 4c plots List of Ideas and None at about the same level.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Type of GPT-4o assistance during three exposure RAT problems: None, LLM Answer (the GPT-4o solution), or LLM Guidance (five associated words per cue word, with GPT-4o instructed not to give the solution directly). The guidance words can include the solution: the Table 2 sample for flake, mobile, cone lists 'snow' among the words for 'flake' (p. 18). The two test problems were unassisted for everyone.
assignment.quote: During the exposure phase, participants were required to solve three RAT problems consecutively. They were randomly assigned to one of three conditions, each providing different types of LLM assistance:
assignment.locator: p. 9, Section 4.1.1; p. 9, Section 4.1 ('three-condition, between-subjects experiment'); p. 9, Figure 7 ('Randomize Condition', '33.3% each')
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 9, footnote 2 (https://aspredicted.org/4q75-bskd.pdf; AsPredicted #189,207, registered 2024/09/07); p. 11, Sections 4.1.4 and 4.1.5

arms.name: None
arms.description: Control group. Also labeled 'No LLM Response' (Figures 7, 8a) and 'No LLM Assistance' (Section 4.2.1).

arms.name: LLM Answer
arms.description: The answer generated by GPT-4o for the given set of words, shown with the compound words (Figure 8b; Table 2). The interface said participants could freely use the AI suggestion.

arms.name: LLM Guidance
arms.description: GPT-4o with a coach system prompt (Figure 12) listed five associated words for each cue word and nudged participants to jot the words down on paper. The model was instructed not to provide the solution directly (p. 9), but the words can include it: one of the three samples in Table 2 (flake, mobile, cone) lists the solution 'snow' first among the words for 'flake' (p. 18).

participants.exclusions: 640 recruited (Figure 7 shows n = 640 entering the flow that leads to randomization, 33.3% each), 'of whom 99% passed the attention check'. The paper does not say whether those who failed were dropped and gives no per-arm or analyzed count; the preregistration (item 6) planned to exclude attention-check failures and non-completers. The ANCOVA error df is 1256 (p. 11).
participants.who: Prolific participants (crowdworkers) based in the US or UK and fluent in English; paid $1.30 for about 10 minutes
participants.quote: We recruited 640 participants from Prolific (of whom 99% passed the attention check).

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o (gpt-4o, date of use August 2024; temperature 0; top-p 0.95; max response 800; frequency and presence penalty 0)
ai_tool.how_used: Static response panel, not an interactive chat, shown 5 seconds after each problem and streamed character by character. The interface said participants could freely use the AI suggestions. LLM Answer gave the solution word with its compounds (ideas_supplied). LLM Guidance listed five associated words per cue word and encouraged participants to find the link. GPT-4o was told not to give the solution directly, but the words can include it ('snow' for flake, mobile, cone; Table 2, p. 18). The paper calls this arm coach-like, but it supplies candidate words, so it does not fit the codebook's coach code, which supplies no content. The role field records the standard arm. No LLM support in the two test problems. Settings in Appendix B.1, p. 16.

task.description: Remote Associates Test (convergent thinking): find a fourth word that forms a compound or phrase with each of three cue words; easy and medium items from Bowden and Jung-Beeman (2003). A one-minute verbal fluency task (covariate), three exposure problems with the assigned assistance, a one-minute Snake distractor game, then two test problems without AI. Participants were never shown the correct answers except inside LLM responses.
task.duration: One minute per problem (exposure rounds held for the full minute; test rounds advanced on submission); about 10 minutes overall

outcomes.name: RAT accuracy, test rounds (unassisted)
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Accuracy on the two test-round RAT problems, each with one correct answer. The paper does not describe how answers were scored. No codebook measure code fits answer-key accuracy: automated_score means a scoring model for creativity (codebook Section 6), so it is a placeholder here until Review 1 adds a code or a convention. ANCOVA of test-round accuracy on condition, controlling for words produced in the verbal fluency task, with Tukey HSD post-hoc tests. The unit is not stated: the error df (1256) exceeds the 640 people recruited, which fits one row per test answer (two per person) with no clustering by participant, while the preregistration defines the DV as the number of correct answers on the two unassisted problems (AsPredicted #189,207, item 3). Figure 9 plots accuracy in percent.
outcomes.delay: Same session, after a one-minute Snake distractor game

contrasts.reported: Omnibus ANCOVA condition F(2, 1256) = 5.134, p = 0.006 (verbal fluency F(1, 1256) = 16.715, p < 0.001); Tukey HSD LLM Guidance vs no LLM responses p = 0.005, mean difference of -10.6 [95% CI: -18.6, -2.7]. No unit is printed for the difference (Figure 9's axis is accuracy in percent), and the paper does not say whether it is adjusted for verbal fluency.
Omnibus F(2, 1256) = 5.134, p = 0.006; Tukey HSD LLM Answer vs No LLM Assistance p = 0.682

Omnibus F(2, 1256) = 5.134, p = 0.006; Tukey HSD LLM Guidance vs LLM Answer p = 0.064, 'a trend suggesting that the LLM Guidance condition performed worse', which 'did not reach statistical significance levels'

outcomes.name: RAT accuracy, exposure rounds (AI available)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Accuracy on the three exposure problems. Figure 9 only (percent accuracy by phase and condition); no test is reported, and the caption does not say what the error bars show. With no analysis, the paper names no unit: output is kept by convention, parallel to S2-O1. The Figure 9 caption calls the plotted values 'participant accuracy' for both phases, including the test phase, where the ANCOVA df implies one row per answer. automated_score is a placeholder for answer-key scoring, as in S2-O1.

contrasts.reported: No statistic printed. Text: 'participants in the LLM Answer condition did better in the Exposure rounds in comparison to the other conditions'; values only in Figure 9.

No text or test. Figure 9 plots LLM Guidance below None in the exposure phase, with error bars that do not overlap. Section 5.1.1 says LLM assistance 'was helpful during the exposure phase' across both experiments, which Figure 9 does not show for LLM Guidance.

company_involvement.description: None stated. All four authors list the University of Toronto (p. 1), and the paper has no funding statement. The Acknowledgments thank Jake Hofman for feedback on the experimental design, Hofman, Dan Goldstein, and David Rothschild for their sports metaphor on human-AI relationships, and Peter Organisciak and his group for access to their automated AUT scoring API; the paper gives no affiliation for any of them. GPT-4o produced the AI responses (Appendices A.1.1 and B.1.1).
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author block; p. 14, Acknowledgments; p. 16, Appendices A.1.1 and B.1.1

eligibility.reason: Both experiments randomly assign individual Prolific participants, between subjects, to no AI or to one of two GPT-4o assistance types for three exposure rounds (p. 4, Section 3.1.1 and Figure 2; p. 9, Section 4.1.1 and Figure 7). Neither prints the number of people analyzed, but 460 and 640 were recruited (pp. 6, 11). Experiment 1 reports no exclusion and analyzes 9,457 ideas. In Experiment 2 the only possible exclusion mentioned is the 1 percent who failed the attention check, and the ANCOVA error df of 1256 implies at least 1,260 rows, which fits one row per test answer and so at least 630 people analyzed (p. 11). Both are far above 50. Outcomes are scored on the outputs: classifier originality, idea counts, and SBERT distances for AUT ideas, and accuracy for RAT answers. Exposure-round outcomes were produced with AI available (with_ai; group-level diversity is across_people), and test-round outcomes without it in the same session (after_ai). The final-pass corrections (S1-O9 construct and unit, the content of the LLM Guidance arm) change no criterion. Experiment 1 is the clearer fit. Experiment 2's outcome is convergent, an open question in codebook Section 13.

one_line_finding: After AI was removed, AUT originality was lower with prior GPT-4o strategies than with no AI (Kruskal-Wallis H(2) = 9.14, p = 0.010; Dunn p = 0.009) and did not differ with prior GPT-4o idea lists (p = 1.000) (p. 7), and RAT accuracy was lower with prior GPT-4o guidance than with no AI (Tukey p = 0.005; mean difference -10.6, 95% CI [-18.6, -2.7]) and did not differ with prior GPT-4o answers (p = 0.682) (p. 11).
open_questions: Analyzed and per-arm counts: neither experiment prints them. Experiment 2 does not say whether the 1 percent who failed the attention check were dropped, and Experiment 1 mentions no attention check, although both preregistrations (item 6) planned to exclude attention-check failures and non-completers. Criterion 2 holds either way (460 recruited with no exclusion reported; at least 630 analyzed in Experiment 2 from the error df).

Unit of analysis: the paper names the observation in no Experiment 1 test. Originality (S1-O1, S1-O2) and creative flexibility (S1-O9) are defined per idea and coded output. Exposure-phase fluency and individual diversity (S1-O4, S1-O6) may be participant-rounds (three per person) or participant means and are coded participant. The Experiment 2 ANCOVA error df (1256) exceeds the 640 people recruited and fits one row per test answer (two per person) with no clustering by participant, while the preregistration defines the DV as the number correct out of two per participant. Exposure-round accuracy (S2-O2) has no test, so its unit is a convention. This matters for standard errors (codebook Section 10), not for eligibility.

Tukey mean difference: the paper does not say whether -10.6 is adjusted for verbal fluency or whether its 95% interval is a simultaneous Tukey interval; this matters for deriving a standard error from the interval.

No arm means, SDs, or standard errors are printed for any outcome. Arm levels exist only in Figures 4, 5, and 9, and the Figure 4 and Figure 9 captions do not say what their error bars show. Extraction will need digitizing or the authors' data.

Group-level diversity: the test phase has no printed test; its error bars come from 150 Monte Carlo resamples, not from participants; the paper does not say how many set-level values enter each arm, and its claim that the 7-idea sample 'reflects the number of participants in each condition' is not explained (460 recruited across three arms). The unit is coded set, the nearest code; the codebook's unit list has no code for a resampled 7-idea subset.

Choice of primary contrast: codebook rule 3 picks the arm closest to free chatbot use (List of Ideas, LLM Answer; Figure 1 calls the standard arm 'analogous to using a chat LLM such as ChatGPT'), whereas the paper's significant after_ai effects are for the coach-like arms (List of Strategies, LLM Guidance). This is a Review 1 decision.

Should RAT accuracy (convergent, one correct answer) enter beside rated creativity (codebook Section 13)? The codebook lists convergent as a construct, and the paper's eligibility rests on Experiment 1 in any case.

Measure code for RAT accuracy (S2-O1, S2-O2): no codebook measure code fits answer-key accuracy, and the paper does not say how answers were scored. automated_score is a placeholder until Review 1 adds a code or a convention.

LLM Guidance content: the paper does not report how often the guidance words contained the solution. One of the three Table 2 samples does ('snow' for flake, mobile, cone, p. 18). This bears on reading LLM Guidance as a coach arm and on the LLM Guidance vs LLM Answer contrast.

Creative flexibility (S1-O9): the paper implies, but does not state, that the Exposure set holds the participant's own exposure-round ideas. The outcome is coded flexibility; novelty (p-creativity) is the alternative reading.
Version check: confirm that the ACM CHI '25 version of record matches arXiv v2. arXiv v2 is the latest preprint version, but the ACM file was not compared.
notes: Version on file is arXiv v2 (15 Feb 2025) in CHI '25 camera-ready format; the version of record is DOI 10.1145/3706598.3714198. The AI was a fixed GPT-4o response panel, not open chat. Each AI arm vs no AI is ai_vs_bau; List of Strategies vs List of Ideas and LLM Guidance vs LLM Answer are ai_design with the coach-like arm as treatment, listed only where the paper prints a pairwise result. ai_tool.role records the standard arm (ideas_supplied). The Experiment 1 List of Strategies arm fits coach (Figure 11: 'Don't include any examples, but only prompts or questions to help users ideate'). The Experiment 2 LLM Guidance arm, which the paper calls coach-like, lists candidate words that can include the solution (Table 2, p. 18), so it does not fit coach, which supplies no content; no field records its role. Individual-level idea diversity (S1-O5, S1-O6) and the paper's 'creative flexibility' (S1-O9) are coded flexibility, as variety among one person's own ideas. Only the group-level Monte Carlo measure is coded diversity. Primary status: test-round originality (Experiment 1) and test-round RAT accuracy (Experiment 2) are the preregistered main questions and key DVs (paper Sections 3.1.4, 4.1.4, 4.1.5; AsPredicted #189,206 and #189,207, items 2-3). The Experiment 1 preregistration lists participant- and group-level diversity and the number of ideas as additional analyses (item 8), and creative flexibility is not preregistered, so these are secondary; Figure 1's 'primary measures' separates the unassisted round from the exposure rounds, which the question codes already record. statistics_available lists test_statistic for every pairwise contrast whose outcome and phase has a printed omnibus Kruskal-Wallis H or ANCOVA F, and 'reported' labels it omnibus; Dunn and Tukey results are printed as p-values only, except the Tukey interval for LLM Guidance vs None. Self-reported outcomes are not listed because they are not scored on the output: change in self-perceived creativity, change in attitudes toward AI, perceived test difficulty, and perceived helpfulness of the exposure rounds (Figure 6, p. 8; Figure 10, p. 12). Figure 3 (p. 5) labels the Experiment 1 arms 'LLM Answer' and 'LLM Guidance'. The Figure 10 caption opens with 'Plots of participant accuracy on the Remote Associates Task', but its panels show the self-reports. The 'Figure ??' on p. 10 is a broken reference in the PDF itself (it points to the sample responses in Table 2). The abstract's 1,100 participants is 460 + 640. Final pass (10/5/2026): the three challenge files (assignment, people, outcome) were checked against the PDF pages, the markdown, and both AsPredicted preregistrations; final.challenge_resolution lists each decision.

open_items.item: Analyzed and per-arm counts: neither experiment prints them. Experiment 2 does not say whether the 1 percent who failed the attention check were dropped, and Experiment 1 mentions no attention check, although both preregistrations (item 6) planned to exclude attention-check failures and non-completers. Criterion 2 holds either way (460 recruited with no exclusion reported; at least 630 analyzed in Experiment 2 from the error df).

Unit of analysis: the paper names the observation in no Experiment 1 test. Originality (S1-O1, S1-O2) and creative flexibility (S1-O9) are defined per idea and coded output. Exposure-phase fluency and individual diversity (S1-O4, S1-O6) may be participant-rounds (three per person) or participant means and are coded participant. The Experiment 2 ANCOVA error df (1256) exceeds the 640 people recruited and fits one row per test answer (two per person) with no clustering by participant, while the preregistration defines the DV as the number correct out of two per participant. Exposure-round accuracy (S2-O2) has no test, so its unit is a convention. This matters for standard errors (codebook Section 10), not for eligibility.

Tukey mean difference: the paper does not say whether -10.6 is adjusted for verbal fluency or whether its 95% interval is a simultaneous Tukey interval; this matters for deriving a standard error from the interval.

No arm means, SDs, or standard errors are printed for any outcome. Arm levels exist only in Figures 4, 5, and 9, and the Figure 4 and Figure 9 captions do not say what their error bars show. Extraction will need digitizing or the authors' data.

Group-level diversity: the test phase has no printed test; its error bars come from 150 Monte Carlo resamples, not from participants; the paper does not say how many set-level values enter each arm, and its claim that the 7-idea sample 'reflects the number of participants in each condition' is not explained (460 recruited across three arms). The unit is coded set, the nearest code; the codebook's unit list has no code for a resampled 7-idea subset.

Choice of primary contrast: codebook rule 3 picks the arm closest to free chatbot use (List of Ideas, LLM Answer; Figure 1 calls the standard arm 'analogous to using a chat LLM such as ChatGPT'), whereas the paper's significant after_ai effects are for the coach-like arms (List of Strategies, LLM Guidance). This is a Review 1 decision.

Should RAT accuracy (convergent, one correct answer) enter beside rated creativity (codebook Section 13)? The codebook lists convergent as a construct, and the paper's eligibility rests on Experiment 1 in any case.

Measure code for RAT accuracy (S2-O1, S2-O2): no codebook measure code fits answer-key accuracy, and the paper does not say how answers were scored. automated_score is a placeholder until Review 1 adds a code or a convention.

LLM Guidance content: the paper does not report how often the guidance words contained the solution. One of the three Table 2 samples does ('snow' for flake, mobile, cone, p. 18). This bears on reading LLM Guidance as a coach arm and on the LLM Guidance vs LLM Answer contrast.

Creative flexibility (S1-O9): the paper implies, but does not state, that the Exposure set holds the participant's own exposure-round ideas. The outcome is coded flexibility; novelty (p-creativity) is the alternative reading.
Version check: confirm that the ACM CHI '25 version of record matches arXiv v2. arXiv v2 is the latest preprint version, but the ACM file was not compared.
